title: Occupational Burnout is a Thing, According to the World Health Organization https://davestuartjr.com/occupational-burnout-is-a-thing-according-to-the-world-health-organization
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Writing originally in early 2020 and re-published as newly relevant amid COVID school closures, Dave Stuart Jr. uses the WHO's ICD-11 definition of occupational burnout — exhaustion, cynicism or mental distance from one's job, and reduced professional efficacy — to validate teachers' experience of chronic workplace stress and reframe it as a manageable, not inevitable, condition. He argues teachers aren't uniquely burned out; rather, unmanaged 'always-on' habits, like constant email checking and bringing work home, are what turn ordinary job stress into chronic burnout. Drawing on Lead Yourself First by Raymond Kethledge and Michael Erwin, he holds up historical figures like Dwight Eisenhower and Jane Goodall as models of thriving under pressure through the practice of solitude. The piece closes by normalizing burnout as a common teaching-profession experience while insisting teachers retain agency to set boundaries and manage stress deliberately.
points: WHO's ICD-11 defines occupational burnout by three specific symptoms — energy depletion, increased cynicism or mental distance from the job, and reduced professional efficacy — giving teachers vocabulary to name and validate what they're experiencing.

Burnout isn't unique to teaching; it results from chronic, unmanaged workplace stress that any 'always-on' professional can develop, especially when personal boundaries around email, devices, and take-home work erode.

Stuart's practice of 'starting with the constraint' (echoing Cal Newport's 'fixed-schedule productivity') — scheduling available time first and prioritizing work within it, rather than letting workload dictate hours — is offered as a concrete defense against chronic stress.
Kethledge and Erwin's Lead Yourself First is cited as evidence that solitude, not innate resilience, is what let high-pressure figures like Eisenhower and Goodall flourish under sustained stress.
The piece explicitly grants teachers permission to 'turn it off,' reframing boundary-setting as professional rather than a failure of dedication.
quotes: The teacher who works in an undisciplined manner — without boundaries, with no constraints — will experience chronic stress. It's like a law of human nature. There is no way around it.

In their latest revision of the International Classification of Diseases (ICD-11), WHO explains that 'occupational burnout' is not a disease, but that it is a growing reason that people seek medical attention.
What causes this syndrome? According to WHO, occupational burnout results 'from chronic workplace stress that has not been successfully managed.'

First, sometimes we teachers think that we're unique in the experience of burnout, but we're not. While there are unique ways in which teaching produces chronic stress (e.g., feeling the weight of the world's future on your shoulders along with the weight of 38,000 forms of documentation and data and standards and certification you're supposed to keep track of), the experience of chronic stress in our jobs isn't unique to teachers.
That word 'chronic' is important. One reason chronic occupational stress is on the rise is because, if you let yourself, you can be tied to the job 24/7.

No. It was solitude — an ancient discipline that our hyper-connected world has all but forgotten. If you're feeling the burn of occupational burnout right now, consider the audio version of Lead Yourself First.
Finally, let me say that if you're experiencing occupational burnout right now, you're not alone. It's more common in teaching than its absence is!
There are things we can do to get better at managing the stress of teaching. We do have agency, even amidst the pressure.
